newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-FRAIL INDIAN WOMAN KEEPS GANDHI'S IDEALS ALIVE.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-FRAIL INDIAN WOMAN KEEPS GANDHI'S IDEALS ALIVE.

text.p: Modern India may have lost sight of the ideals of truth and simplicity preached by founding father Mahatma Gandhi but a frail white-haired lady still perseveres, leading the movement from her Bombay study.
Usha Mehta is 77, her skin almost as translucent as the thin white handspun cotton saris she has worn since first meeting Mahatma Gandhi as a child.
His teachings prompted Mehta to throw herself energetically into India's freedom movement. She became one of its first underground disc jockeys.

"The first slogan I shouted against the British was 'Simon go back'," Mehta told Reuters in a recent interview, referring to a 1928 protest rally she joined to oppose a government panel chaired by Sir John Simon.
The panel was set up to suggest Indian constitutional reforms.
"I was eight years-old then," she added, her mellow voice trailing off into reminiscence. "We young girls had formed a 'Cats' Army' to participate in the freedom struggle.
"We followed our elders, though we hardly understood what it was. We were the front-runners in shouting slogans."
INDIA WAKES TO NEW APPRECIATION OF MEHTA

In its golden jubilee year as a free nation, India has awakened to a fresh appreciation of Mehta's role. The harsh glare of publicity has illumined the book- lined study from where she has steered the Gandhian movement for more than 40 years.
Mehta's moment of glory came in 1942, when Gandhi and his Congress political party launched a campaign to force the British to "Quit India".

"Violence and repression rose to their peak at this time of terror, fear and hatred," historian Stanley Wolpert wrote of the campaign. "The British treated it as an open rebellion, arresting some 60,000 Congress supporters by the end of 1942."
For three months at the peak of the campaign, Mehta broadcast daily news bulletins from a secret mobile transmitter, constantly shifting location to elude police.
Many of the movement's leaders had been arrested, and in the initial stages Mehta and her colleagues could only play the records of their speeches at political meetings.
"And of course, before we could contact them, we used to play only the records of speeches -- Gandhi's speech, Nehru's speech, Maulana Azad's speech, so somehow we managed," Mehta said.

"We had to change from place to place because there was a detecting van that the government had put after us," Mehta added. "The van could give them the direction but not the exact location. So, by the time they got one direction, we had shifted to the other place."
BETRAYED, THE BROADCASTERS SHUT DOWN
But the authorities cracked down hard. A technician betrayed the team and led police to the site. Broadcasts shut down.
"By the time we had finished the programme, the police came, and they broke open three doors," Mehta says of the day she was arrested. "There was a battalion of police, 150 of them."
Mehta paid a high price. She served a four-year jail term, during which an intestinal disease destroyed her digestive system, leaving her unable to consume virtually any solid food.
"I have had just two cups of tea and one cup of coffee throughout the day today," she said. "That's how I survive."
Today, Mehta is ready to modify the stern Gandhian emphasis on self-reliance, but pleads fervently for the protection of indigenous cottage industries.
"Liberalisation, yes. Globalisation, yes. You have to keep pace with the changing world," Mehta said.
"But at the same time you must see to it that your indigenous industries and crafts do not suffer, and that those who already have some work are not deprived of it.
GANDHIAN VALUES ARE ETERNAL

The tumultuous events since 1947 have discouraged Mehta, but have not quenched her spirit. Corruption and nepotism have emerged as the dominant themes of Indian politics, tarnishing the rosy optimism that accompanied the dawn of freedom.
"Every day I feel that now we cannot go any lower than this. But the next day they do find out some means," she said.
Yet Mehta refuses to cut Gandhi's philosophy to the cloth of Indian political demands.

Gandhi's philosophy would always retain its relevance, she said. "There are two things we must remember: one, the whole world is coming to realise that there is no other way for permanent and lasting peace.

"Secondly, Gandhi's non-violence was certainly love. It was hatelessness, spitelessness, but at the same time it (means) not yielding to any injustice," Mehta added. "If any injustice is being done you must have the courage to protest and for that he was even willing to accept violence in self-defence."
